name: Esther Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm lead carpenter for a renovation firm that does old townhouses in the historic part of town, most of them over a hundred years old. Right now I'm rebuilding a staircase that's been patched by about five different people since 1910, and replacing sash windows with exact copies. I get in at half seven, have a coffee in the van, and then it's a lot of measuring, a lot of head-scratching and then very careful cutting. Nothing in those houses is straight, not one wall.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment you find the original carpenter's pencil marks under the paint, and you know you're the next one in line. What wears me out is clients who want it done in two weeks when it took a man a year in 1910. And the dust, you never get rid of the dust. I'm not on social media much and I don't use any of the AI things, my phone does calls, photos and the weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: All right, the first one. This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's that then, and go back to my staircase. I'm not the type to post about it. If somebody at the yard brought it up I'd probably say I never thought a computer could plane a sash anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel a bit lucky. My husband Marco's an accountant, and he's been the one worrying, not me. If it fizzles, he can stop reading articles at the dinner table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Exactly what I'm doing now. Keep working, keep the savings where they are, which is about eight months plus Marco's pension. We were going to replace the car next year, and we'd just go ahead with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like nothing happened, because in my world nothing did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Marco read out at dinner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Headlines about AI doing tax returns, mostly. Sofia, she's thirteen, she rolls her eyes and Mateo asks if a robot can do his homework. I usually change the subject to whose turn it is to do the dishes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI stays small, is there anything in your work you'd still worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finding people. The old skills are dying out, there's maybe three of us in town who can make a proper sash window. That's my worry, not robots, it's who carries this on after me.

S0.say: She'd say "that's that, then" and go back to her staircase without posting anything. At the yard she'd say she never thought a computer could plane a sash window anyway.
S0.think: Privately she'd feel lucky, mostly for her husband, an accountant who has been the worried one. She'd be glad he could stop reading AI headlines at dinner.
S0.do: Keeps working exactly as now and leaves about eight months of savings untouched. Goes ahead with replacing the family car next year as planned.
S0.feel: Calm, as if nothing happened, because in her world nothing did.
S0.quote: There's maybe three of us in town who can make a proper sash window. That's my worry, not robots, it's who carries this on after me.
S0.fieldNote: Esther lives in a world of irregular old buildings where she sees no role for machines. She is matter-of-fact and avoids the topic at home. Her real worry is who will inherit her rare skills, which she raised unprompted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it makes sense for some jobs, and old houses aren't one of them. I'd tell people that nobody's sending a robot up a ladder into a hundred-year-old roof. And I'd say it'll be up to each person to deal with it, that's just how things go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm fine. It's Marco I'd be worried about, because he does the books for small businesses, and that's exactly the kind of thing a computer can learn. If he lost half his clients, we'd still be all right, but the house was bought on two incomes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Marco to start looking now at what else he could do, and maybe I'd put more into savings, a couple of hundred a month. Me, I wouldn't change anything at work. I'd wait and see who in my trade actually gets affected before I start learning anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not about the staircase, about the kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You told Marco to look at other options. Would you take the same advice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and I can hear how that sounds. But I genuinely don't think a machine is coming for what I do in the next few years. I'll change when I can see it coming down the street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at the yard if a younger carpenter asked about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn the old stuff properly, the joinery, because that's what's rare. Let everyone else run after the gadgets. Somebody has to know how to fix a house that a robot can't measure.

S1.say: She'd say AI makes sense for some jobs but not old house restoration, because no robot is going up a ladder into a century-old roof. She'd add that each person has to deal with it themselves.
S1.think: Privately she feels safe but worries about her husband, whose bookkeeping work is easy for AI to learn. They'd cope, but their house was bought on two incomes.
S1.do: Urges her husband to explore other work and adds a couple of hundred a month to savings. Changes nothing in her own work and waits to see who in her trade gets affected before learning anything.
S1.feel: Uneasy, not about her own work but about the family budget.
S1.quote: Not about the staircase, about the kitchen table.
S1.fieldNote: Her worry here is entirely through her husband's exposure. When the gap between her advice to him and to herself was named, she admitted it plainly and stuck to her view. Her centre outlook shows in putting it down to each person rather than blaming anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, out loud, that I don't believe it, not in two years, not for old buildings. That's probably what I'd say until the day the robot turned up. Then I'd say the government had better have a plan, because I don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one frightens me. If it can do almost any work, then both Marco and I are out at the same time, and that's the mortgage, the kids, everything. I wouldn't know where to start, I've done this one thing since I was sixteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the car, stop the holiday, and we'd live on Marco's salary as long as it lasted and put mine straight into savings. I'd call my brother, he's got a smallholding out past the reservoir, and ask if we could go there if it got bad. I wouldn't retrain, I wouldn't even know what to retrain in. I'd keep working on whatever jobs were still left, because old houses don't renovate themselves overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sofia and Mateo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we've got savings and a family, and that's more than most. I wouldn't tell them I was scared, I'd tell Marco. Sofia would figure it out anyway, she's sharp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying you wouldn't know what to retrain in. If someone gave you a list, would you look?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look. I'd probably put it on the fridge and look at it for a month. That's the honest answer, I'm slow with this stuff and I know it.

S2.say: She'd say publicly she doesn't believe it, not in two years and not for old buildings, until a robot actually turned up. Then she'd say the government had better have a plan, because she doesn't.
S2.think: Privately it frightens her, because she and her husband could lose work at the same time. Having done one craft since sixteen, she wouldn't know where to start.
S2.do: Cancels the car and holiday, lives on her husband's salary and banks her own pay. Asks her brother if the family could move to his smallholding if things got bad, and keeps taking whatever renovation work is left without retraining.
S2.quote: I'd probably put it on the fridge and look at it for a month.
S2.fieldNote: Her public denial and private fear sit far apart in this scenario. Strong savings soften but don't remove the threat of both incomes going at once. She is unusually honest about her slowness with change and leans on family rather than the state.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a long time, a lot can change, let's see. I'd say it in a calm voice, because that's how I talk. People at the yard would probably say the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd know I'd probably waste the first two years telling myself it wasn't real. Then I'd panic in year three. I know myself, that's what I did with the dentist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay down the mortgage harder, maybe four hundred extra a month, and tell Marco to start a second string, because he's better at that than me. I'd keep working on the townhouses as long as clients wanted me. And I'd talk to Sofia about what she studies, because she'd be eighteen right when it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. More awake at night than in the slow one, less than the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sofia to study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something with people, a nurse, a teacher, a lawyer maybe. Or something old and rare like me, but I wouldn't wish that on her. I don't really know, and I'd tell her that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, it's a punch. With five, it's a slow leak in the roof, you know you should fix it and you keep putting the bucket under. I'd use the time on money, not on me.

S3.say: She'd say calmly that five years is a long time and a lot can change. People at the yard would likely say the same thing.
S3.think: Privately she knows she'd waste the first two years in denial and panic in the third. She compares it to how she handles going to the dentist.
S3.do: Pays about four hundred extra a month into the mortgage and urges her husband to build a second income. Keeps working on townhouses and talks with her daughter about what to study.
S3.feel: Anxious, more than in steady change and less than in the two-year version.
S3.quote: With five, it's a slow leak in the roof, you know you should fix it and you keep putting the bucket under.
S3.fieldNote: Esther is self-aware about her avoidance and predicts her own procrastination. She uses the extra time on money rather than skills. Again she pushes her husband to adapt while staying put herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long way off and I'm not going to worry about something that far away. I'd say people have been predicting robots for forty years. That's the public me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still worry, because I know I wouldn't do much with the time. Ten years from now I'm fifty-three, and I'd have spent most of it hoping it wouldn't happen. Then it happens and I'm fifty-three with one skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd probably carry on as I am for the first five years and save. Maybe somewhere around year six I'd look at teaching restoration, because I know that's rare and colleges might still want a person for it. The mortgage would be close to done by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, which surprises me. I thought ten years would feel safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why doesn't ten years feel safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know what I'm like. Time doesn't help me if I don't use it, and I don't. Marco would use it, he'd have three plans by Christmas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If someone came to your yard and offered a paid course on working with robots, would you go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they paid me and it was on a Saturday, I'd go once. If it made sense, I'd go back. I'm slow, not stupid.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is too far away to worry about and that people have predicted robots for forty years. That's her public line.
S4.think: Privately she'd still worry, because she knows she wouldn't use the time well. She fears reaching fifty-three with only one skill after a decade of hoping it wouldn't happen.
S4.do: Carries on as now for about five years while saving and paying down the mortgage. Considers teaching restoration around year six and says she'd try one paid Saturday course if offered.
S4.feel: Still anxious, which surprises her, because she expected ten years to feel safe.
S4.quote: Time doesn't help me if I don't use it, and I don't.
S4.fieldNote: This was the surprise: extra time doesn't calm her, because she trusts herself not to use it. Her mood stays anxious across all three AGI pictures for that reason. Her last line showed pride as well as self-knowledge.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Marco and I would both go at once. What would help is someone telling me exactly what to learn, paid, on a Saturday, close to home. And keeping the restoration skills alive, so there's still a place for people like me in old buildings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the houses. Whoever fixes them next needs to know how they were built. If it's a robot, fine, but somebody has to teach it, and I'd rather it was me than nobody.

portrait: Esther Torres is a 43-year-old lead restoration carpenter working on century-old townhouses, married to an accountant, with two children of thirteen and ten. She never uses AI and believes old, crooked buildings will outlast the machines, though she worries constantly about her husband's more exposed job. She's calm under the plateau, uneasy under steady change and alarmed by AGI in two years, when both incomes could go at once. Longer warning doesn't calm her, because she freely admits she would put off acting until the last minute.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she and her husband would both lose work at once.
whatWouldHelp: Someone telling her exactly what to learn, with paid Saturday training close to home, and keeping restoration skills alive in old buildings.
